- **The real layout of the world (continents, oceans, sea routes)** [`world_geography`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/world_geography.md) — K3, use partial, make medium, accept high. The earth is a sphere; al-Ma'mun's astronomers measure a degree. Al-Khwarizmi is recasting Ptolemy's coordinates in his Picture of the Earth, and a world map is drawn for the caliph. Merchants know the sea route to China; the Encircling Sea bounds the west. Local: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi; al-Ma'mun's world map (al-sura al-ma'muniyya); Basra and Siraf merchants who have been to Khanfu (Guangzhou). Elsewhere: Tang China.
- **Global wind belts and ocean currents (trade winds, westerlies, volta do mar, monsoon)** [`wind_systems_ocean_currents`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/wind_systems_ocean_currents.md) — K3, use correct, make easy, accept high. Gulf captains time their voyages to India and China by the monsoon and count a round trip to China in a year or more. The global wind belts and the Atlantic are beyond anyone's horizon. Local: ship captains (nakhuda) and pilots of Basra, Ubulla and Siraf.

Pilots keep courses by star bearings and reckon distance in days' sail, from memory and oral rutters. No log line, no sandglass, no compass.
- **Latitude from Pole Star and noon Sun (quadrant, astrolabe, cross-staff, kamal)** [`latitude_astrolabe_quadrant`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/latitude_astrolabe_quadrant.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Court astronomers take latitude with astrolabes and quadrants, and the Mumtahan tables give town latitudes. Pilots judge the Pole Star's height by eye; a finger-scaled sighting board is attested only later. Local: Ali ibn Isa al-Asturlabi; Sanad ibn Ali.

- **Sounding lead, rutters and coastal pilotage** [`sounding_lead_pilotage`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/sounding_lead_pilotage.md) — K4, use correct, make easy, accept high. The Shatt al-Arab and the Gulf are full of shoals; pilots sound with lead and line and pass on landmarks orally. Written rutters come centuries later. Local: pilots at Ubulla and Abbadan.
- **Tides and tide tables** [`tides_tide_tables`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/tides_tide_tables.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept medium. Basra's canals fill and empty twice a day with the tide of the Shatt al-Arab, and boatmen and millers time their work by it. The tie to the moon is noticed; a theory and tables are not. Local: Basra's tidal canals.

- **Ocean-going ships (carvel hull, sternpost rudder, mixed square and lateen rig)** [`ship_design_caravel_carrack`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/ship_design_caravel_carrack.md) — K1, use partial, make hard, accept medium. Gulf ships are sewn-plank hulls of Indian teak tied with coconut cord, Their steering and rig in this century are uncertain; later pictures show square sails. A sewn ship of this kind sinks off Belitung about now, full of Chinese bowls. Local: shipwrights at Siraf, Sohar and Ubulla. Elsewhere: Belitung wreck (Java Sea), a sewn ship lost c. 830 with Tang ceramics, one bowl dated 826.
- **Chinese junk and Zheng He's treasure fleets** [`chinese_junk_treasure_ships`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/chinese_junk_treasure_ships.md) — K1, use none, make hard, accept low. Sewn hulls have one open hold. Chinese boats with compartments exist but are not known here. Elsewhere: Tang China, compartmented hulls.
- **Shipworm and copper sheathing** [`copper_sheathing_shipworm`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/copper_sheathing_shipworm.md) — K2, use partial, make medium, accept medium. Shipworm and rot are a constant cost in warm seas; hulls are smeared with oil and lime (described by later writers). Copper is expensive and would need nails a sewn hull does not have.
- **Provisioning and keeping crews alive on long voyages** [`ship_provisioning_long_voyages`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/ship_provisioning_long_voyages.md) — K3, use partial, make easy, accept high. Ships to China stop at Muscat, Quilon and the Malay ports for water and food; dates, rice and dried fish keep. Scurvy is rare on these hops.

Later writers describe wooden beacon platforms (khashabat) in the sea off Abbadan, lit at night for ships entering the Tigris; whether they stand yet is unknown. Elsewhere: Alexandria, the Pharos.

Elsewhere: Bahrain and the Gulf pearl banks.
- **Canals and pound locks** [`canal_locks`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/canal_locks.md) — K1, use none, make medium, accept medium. Iraq's canals are flat and fed by sluices and weirs; boats are towed. A pound lock is unknown and would mainly help where canals cross a level change.

The Khurasan road and the pilgrim road to Mecca (Darb Zubayda, with cisterns and stations) are tracks with wells and inns, not paved. Camel caravans need no pavement. Local: Khurasan road from Baghdad's eastern gate; Darb Zubayda to Mecca.
- **Spoked wheels, pivoting axles and sprung carriages** [`spoked_wheel_suspension_carriage`](https://blueprintsfromtomorrow.com/techtree/generated/tech/spoked_wheel_suspension_carriage.md) — K2, use partial, make medium, accept low.
